proposals.quote_modern: there is not one of his subjects but has forgotten Odysseus
proposals.replacement: every one of his subjects has forgotten Odysseus
proposals.butler: there is not one of his subjects but has forgotten Ulysses
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (syntax, unsure): “archaic ‘not one... but has’ construction; on a quick read it can flip to ‘not one has forgotten him’.” The paraphrase (“every one of them has forgotten him”) is right, but only after reconstructing the construction.
proposals.reason: ‘Not one … but has’ (= not one who has not) is dead syntax. Read with the modern ‘but’, it says that no subject has forgotten him, and that reverses the logic of Athena’s complaint: a good king has been forgotten, so kings may as well be cruel. Homer’s sense is ‘no one of the people he ruled remembers him’ (5.11–12). The repair keeps Butler’s ‘one of his subjects’ and ‘has forgotten Odysseus’ and says the universal outright; ‘every one’ keeps the one-by-one emphasis of ‘not one … but’. Nothing is added or lost.
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶1 contains no ‘every’ (only ‘everlasting’), and no other Butler word in the paragraph is reused. Cross-Book: Mentor’s speech in Book 2 (B02-P014 in the glossary’s 1-based IDs) repeats this Butler sentence (Od. 2.233–234). If this is adopted, the lead should check that accepted Book for the same construction.

proposals.quote_modern: that do their business in the waters
proposals.replacement: whose business is in the waters
proposals.butler: chattering sea-crows that occupy their business in the waters
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (word, MISREAD): “In modern English ‘do their business’ means going to the toilet, so the line reads as unintended toilet humour.” The reader got the intended sense (birds that make their living on the sea) only by reading past the idiom.
proposals.reason: Ruling, made against Butler’s original: the modern text caused this, not Butler. Butler’s ‘occupy their business in the waters’ echoes Psalm 107:23 (‘that do business in great waters’) and renders Homer’s sea-crows ‘to whom the works of the sea are a care’ (5.66–67), birds whose work is on the water. The candidate dropped Butler’s dead verb ‘occupy’ and was left with ‘do their business’. For animals, the dominant present-day sense of that phrase is excretion, so the text now says the birds foul the water: a wrong image and an unintended joke in the Book’s set-piece description. ‘whose business is in the waters’ keeps Butler’s own noun and his ‘in the waters’ (D29). It drops only the idiom and has no scatological reading.
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶5 has ‘busy’ (Calypso busy at her loom) and ‘went’ (Hermes went inside), which rules out ‘busy themselves’ and ‘go about their business’. ‘business’ is Butler’s own word for this thing, and ‘whose’ does not occur.

proposals.butler: He fenced the raft all round with wicker hurdles as a protection against the waves
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (word, unsure): “woven panels of branches set up as a fence or screen along the sides”; note: “modern ‘hurdles’ suggests athletics obstacles”. Book-level note: the raft “cannot be pictured”.
proposals.reason: Butler’s hurdles are portable panels of woven withies used as fencing (Homer 5.256–257: osier wickerwork ‘to be a bulwark against the wave’). To a present-day reader, and an American one especially, ‘hurdles’ are track obstacles or difficulties, so the reader pictures the wrong object even though the sentence still seems to make sense. ‘screens’ names the same object by the function the sentence itself states (‘as a protection against the waves’). ‘wicker’ and Butler’s verb ‘fenced’ stay, so the material and the fencing survive. This replaces one word and keeps the object.
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶19 contains no ‘screen’. Butler’s ‘fenced’ is kept as the verb. ‘wicker fencing’ is rejected because it would make Butler’s verb ‘fenced’ do duty for the object as well.

proposals.quote_modern: making them fast with braces and sheets
proposals.replacement: making them fast with ropes—braces and sheets
proposals.butler: making them fast with braces and sheets
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (word, unsure): “‘sheets’ and ‘braces’ are ropes, not cloth or straps”; note: “right after ‘linen’, ‘sheets’ reads as cloth”.
proposals.reason: Braces and sheets are the ropes that work the yard and the sail (Homer 5.260 names braces, halyards and sheets). They come straight after Calypso’s linen, so ‘sheets’ reads as bedlinen and ‘braces’ as straps, and the sentence seems to say that he fastened cloth with cloth. Both objects are Butler’s concrete detail and are kept. The repair folds one word, ‘ropes’, into the narration at first use to say what kind of thing they are. If the lead would rather add no dividing mark, ‘making them fast with the ropes called braces and sheets’ says the same thing without one.
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶19 contains no ‘rope’ or ‘ropes’. The em dash would be an added sentence-internal mark, recorded under D27/D28. The alternative wording adds no mark.

proposals.quote_modern: pressing me so hard about the dead body of Achilles
proposals.replacement: pressing me so hard around the dead body of Achilles
proposals.butler: the Trojans were pressing me so sorely about the dead body of Achilles
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (syntax, unsure): “In battle the Trojans attacked him fiercely around Achilles’ corpse, as the two sides fought over it; ‘about’ = around, not ‘concerning’.” The reader was only moderately confident.
proposals.reason: Butler’s ‘about’ is spatial: in Homer (5.309–310) the Trojans hurled their spears at him ‘around the dead son of Peleus’. In current English, ‘pressing someone about something’ means pressuring them on a subject. The natural reading is therefore that the Trojans were pestering him over Achilles’ body, not attacking him in the fight around it, which gets the action wrong. ‘around’ restores the spatial sense with one word. ‘so hard’ (the package’s rendering of ‘so sorely’, continuity finding 23.1) is untouched.
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶22 has ‘round’ once, in ‘stirred it round in the sea’. That is a stirring motion and a different word and construction. ‘around’ appears nowhere in Butler’s or the candidate’s paragraph. If the lead counts round and around as one word, ‘over the dead body’ is free of collisions, though weaker, since ‘over’ also reads as ‘concerning’.

proposals.butler: As he spoke a sea broke over him with such terrific fury
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (word, pause): “a huge wave broke over him”; note: “nautical ‘a sea’ = a wave”. The book-level notes list “‘a sea’ for a wave” among the sailing usages.
proposals.reason: ‘a sea’ as a countable noun for one breaking wave is sailors’ usage, and to a landsman ‘a sea broke over him’ reads oddly or as the sea in general. Homer has κῦμα, a wave (5.313). Butler also uses ‘sea’ in this paragraph for the sea itself (‘into the sea’, ‘The sea took the raft’), so the repair separates two senses that he writes with one word. It merges nothing. The two mass uses in ¶22 (‘a tremendous sea got up’, ‘what a sea the winds are raising’) mean the state of the sea, were read correctly, and are kept. The reader decoded this one, so it is optional.
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶23 contains no ‘wave’ or ‘waves’. Butler’s ‘sea’ in the sense of the sea keeps ‘sea’. This separates two senses of one word, which the collision triage classes as context-rendered; it does not merge anything.

proposals.quote_modern: both sail and yard went over
proposals.replacement: both sail and yardarm went over
proposals.butler: both sail and yard went over into the sea
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (word, unsure): “‘yard’ is the sail’s crossbar (the yardarm), not a garden or a measurement.” At ¶19 the reader had noted that the yardarm is “needed again in paragraph 23 (‘yard’)”.
proposals.reason: On its own, ‘yard’ reads as a garden or as three feet, and then ‘sail and yard went over into the sea’ describes nothing. It is the spar Butler calls ‘yard arm’ when Odysseus makes it in ¶19 (candidate ‘yardarm’, which the reader decoded), and Homer uses one word for it in both places (ἐπίκριον, 5.254 and 5.318). Reusing the ¶19 word restores the link and the picture (the mast snapped, the sail and its spar gone) with one word.
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶23 contains neither ‘arm’ nor ‘yardarm’, and ‘yard’ occurs only here. Butler’s ‘yard arm’ (¶19) and ‘yard’ (¶23) name the same spar, so rendering both as ‘yardarm’ does not merge a distinction he keeps.

proposals.butler: Then the god staid his stream and stilled the waves
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (word, pause): “the river god held back / stopped his current”; note: “archaic ‘stayed’ = halted”. The book-level notes list it among the Victorian survivals.
proposals.reason: ‘stay’ in the sense ‘stop’ is dead (it is on the brief’s sweep list). In current English, ‘the god stayed his stream’ either fails to parse or means ‘remained’. Homer: ‘he stopped his current and held back the wave’ (5.451). The edition already renders Butler’s ‘stay’ (= stop) as ‘stop’ elsewhere: 3 ¶26 ‘stopped them’, 4 ¶2 ‘stopped their horses’, 24 ¶42 ‘did not stop it’. This instance survived only because the package treated ‘staid’ → ‘stayed’ as a spelling change (continuity §5). ‘stopped his stream and stilled the waves’ also keeps Butler’s st-/st- pairing. The reader decoded it, so it is optional, but it brings the edition into line with itself.
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶34 uses ‘back’ (‘threw it back into the salt stream’), which rules out ‘held back’. ‘stop’ does not occur there. ‘stilled’ is kept.

proposals.replacement: hides a burning brand as fire-seed
proposals.butler: hides a brand as fire-seed in the ashes to save himself from having to get a light elsewhere
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (imagery, unsure): “A ‘brand’ is a burning stick or ember…”; note: “‘brand’ reads as a trademark; ‘fire-seed’ and ‘get a light’ need thought”. The book-level notes list ‘brand’ among the words whose modern meaning misleads.
proposals.reason: The Book’s last simile turns on this object. A man buries a smoldering piece of firewood in the ashes to keep his fire alive, as Odysseus buries himself in leaves (Homer 5.488–490, δαλός). The dominant present-day sense of ‘brand’ is a trademark, so the simile’s key noun means nothing until the reader works back from ‘ashes’. One adjective, folded into the narration, makes the sense unmistakable and keeps Butler’s noun, ‘fire-seed’ and the whole image.
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶36 contains no ‘burning’. ‘fire’ occurs only inside Butler’s ‘fire-seed’, which is kept. ‘firebrand’ is rejected because it would echo ‘fire-seed’ in the same clause.

rejected_barriers.quote: Dawn rose from her couch beside Tithonus
rejected_barriers.reason: A name and myth from outside this Book (Tithonus). Butler’s reference is kept, and it is not a wording problem.

rejected_barriers.quote: herald of light to mortals and immortals alike
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s apposition, in Butler’s position. The reader attached it to Dawn with high confidence, so this is a pause, not a misreading, and moving it would reorder Butler’s sentence with no failure to justify it.

rejected_barriers.quote: I hope there may never be such a thing as a kind and well-disposed ruler any more
rejected_barriers.reason: Athena’s bitter irony is Homer’s rhetoric, and the reader read it correctly from the ‘for’ clause.

rejected_barriers.quote: lying in great pain
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s words (Homer: ‘lies suffering mighty pains’). The reader settled the meaning from context, and there is no false friend.

rejected_barriers.quote: wicked people are trying to murder
rejected_barriers.reason: The suitors are introduced in Books 1–4, so this is not a defect of Book 5.

rejected_barriers.quote: Did you not send him there yourself
rejected_barriers.reason: A pronoun reference the reader resolved with high confidence. The pronoun is Butler’s.

rejected_barriers.quote: the suitors
rejected_barriers.reason: The suitors are introduced in Books 1–4 (see the context note), so this is not a defect of Book 5.

rejected_barriers.quote: because you thought it would help Odysseus to get home and punish the suitors
rejected_barriers.reason: The plot logic is set up in Books 1–2, and nothing in the wording hides it.

rejected_barriers.quote: the suitors have to come hurrying and scurrying back without having killed him
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly. The statement is Butler’s, and there is no wording issue.

rejected_barriers.quote: near of kin to the gods
rejected_barriers.reason: Recoverable and in register. The reader glossed it exactly, and the edition keeps ‘near of kin’ at 7 ¶17 as well.

rejected_barriers.quote: if he had had all his prize money
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s word. ‘from Troy’ fixes the sense (his share of the spoil, Homer 5.40), which the reader supplied, and the modern sense ‘winnings’ is close enough not to mislead.

rejected_barriers.quote: slayer of Argus
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s epithet for Hermes, kept under the glossary’s epithet rule. It needs outside knowledge only.

rejected_barriers.quote: like a cormorant that flies fishing every hole and corner of the ocean
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s image, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: many a weary wave
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s poetic phrase in the edition’s register. The meaning was recovered: the weariness belongs to the long crossing.

rejected_barriers.quote: shooting her golden shuttle through the warp
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s concrete weaving detail, which the reader decoded.

rejected_barriers.quote: A vine loaded with grapes was trained
rejected_barriers.reason: The current gardening sense, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: channels cut fairly close together, and turned this way and that
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s picture of the garden, read correctly (four streams turned different ways). There is no archaism.

rejected_barriers.quote: but come inside, and let me set refreshment before you
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s own wording (Homer: ‘follow me further in’), so the small tension is already in the source. The paraphrase is right, and this is not the edition’s to fix.

rejected_barriers.quote: a table loaded with ambrosia beside him and mixed him some red nectar
rejected_barriers.reason: The text itself glosses ambrosia and nectar as the gods’ food at ¶15, and nectar is mixed like wine. The wording is Butler’s, with no problem in it.

rejected_barriers.quote: We are speaking god and goddess to one another
rejected_barriers.reason: The implied link was read correctly. Butler’s wording.

rejected_barriers.quote: sacrifices or choice victims
rejected_barriers.reason: Kept, though it was considered. ‘victims’ is the package’s word, not Butler’s (his ‘hecatombs’ is barred by D3). The adjacent ‘sacrifices’ selects the sacrificial sense, which is current (‘sacrificial victim’); the reader glossed it correctly with high confidence; and the edition keeps Butler’s own sacrificial ‘victims’ at 3 ¶25–26. The obvious alternatives collide: ‘offerings’ with Butler’s ‘offer’ in the same sentence, and ‘great sacrifices’ (the D3 form used elsewhere) with his ‘sacrifices’. If the lead still wants a change, ‘choice beasts’ is collision-free inside ¶8.

rejected_barriers.quote: the city of King Priam
rejected_barriers.reason: A name that needs outside knowledge. Butler’s wording.

rejected_barriers.quote: they sinned against Athena, who raised both wind and waves against them
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s (and Homer’s, 5.108–109) account of the storm. The tension the reader notices, with Athena’s championing of Odysseus and with ¶9 and ¶22, is in the source. The poem is not to be fixed.

rejected_barriers.quote: yielded to him in a thrice-plowed fallow field
rejected_barriers.reason: The prior screening ruling (2026-09-23) is upheld: this is Butler’s ‘thrice-ploughed’ with only the D9 spelling changed. The reader understood the literal field, the point of the detail is Homer’s, and ‘yielded’ is a transparent euphemism. No comprehension failure outweighs the ruling.

rejected_barriers.quote: sitting all alone astride a keel
rejected_barriers.reason: Nautical, but decoded correctly (clinging to the keel of the wreck). Butler’s concrete detail.

rejected_barriers.quote: for Zeus had struck his ship with lightning
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s and Homer’s differing accounts of the wreck. They are not the edition’s to reconcile.

rejected_barriers.quote: it was she, not he, who would have it so
rejected_barriers.reason: Recoverable (‘wanted it so’) and read correctly. Butler’s idiom in the edition’s register.

rejected_barriers.quote: a large raft with an upper deck
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s raft (Homer’s decking fixed high on it). The reader paused to picture it but did not misread.

rejected_barriers.quote: if the gods in heaven so will it—for they know more about these things, and can settle them better than I can
rejected_barriers.reason: The divine hierarchy is the poem’s, and it was read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: well-found ship
rejected_barriers.reason: A nautical adjective that is still current, decoded correctly (‘well-equipped’). The sailing vocabulary is Butler’s concrete detail.

rejected_barriers.quote: you mean me no mischief
rejected_barriers.reason: Recoverable. Calypso’s reply in the next paragraph (‘I mean you no sort of harm’) glosses it, and the edition keeps ‘mean me mischief’ at 10 ¶24 and 10 ¶26. Changing it to ‘harm’ would also merge Butler’s two words across ¶13–¶14.

rejected_barriers.quote: the waters of the river Styx
rejected_barriers.reason: A name. The text states what matters (the gods’ most solemn oath).

rejected_barriers.quote: her maids
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s. The attendants are in the source, and this is not a wording problem.

rejected_barriers.quote: they laid their hands on the good things that were before them
rejected_barriers.reason: The guest-meal formula carried from the accepted Books (continuity §7), and it was read correctly (‘They started eating’).

rejected_barriers.quote: It makes no difference how anxious you may be to see this wife of yours
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly (however much he longs for his wife, he would stay). The division is round 1’s ruling 5, which split Butler’s 102-word sentence, and it loses no connection the reader could not recover.

rejected_barriers.quote: let this go with the rest
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly (‘add this to the rest’). ‘with the rest’ blocks the ‘forget it’ reading.

rejected_barriers.quote: Presently
rejected_barriers.reason: Kept at every occurrence (5 ¶18, ¶31, ¶34; 6 ¶20). Past-tense narration, and the future tense at 6 ¶20, rule out the ‘currently’ reading, and the reader glossed it correctly. The edition keeps ‘presently’ throughout (the candidates for Books 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 23 and 24), so changing it in Books 5–6 alone would open a cross-Book drift for no gain in comprehension.

rejected_barriers.quote: the rosy-fingered child of morning
rejected_barriers.reason: The dawn formula fixed by the glossary (Book 2 table), read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: a sharp adze
rejected_barriers.reason: The prior screening ruling is upheld: the adze is Butler’s object (continuity §5 kept the object and replaced only the dead verb, ‘adzed’ → ‘trimmed’). The reader decoded it as a woodworking tool, which is all the sentence needs.

rejected_barriers.quote: very dry and well seasoned, so as to sail light for him in the water
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly. Butler’s concrete detail.

rejected_barriers.quote: squaring them by rule
rejected_barriers.reason: A carpentry detail (Homer 5.245: he made them straight to the line), read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: augers
rejected_barriers.reason: The text explains it (‘he bored holes with them’).

rejected_barriers.quote: as broad as a skilled shipwright makes the beam of a large vessel
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly with high confidence. ‘as broad as’ names the dimension, so ‘beam’ meaning width can be recovered. The nautical term is kept as Butler’s concrete detail.

rejected_barriers.quote: fixed a deck on top of the ribs
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly. Kept.

rejected_barriers.quote: ran a gunwale all round it
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly (a raised edge along the sides). Kept as Butler’s object; the pronunciation does not affect comprehension.

rejected_barriers.quote: a mast with a yardarm
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly and kept. The same word is reused at ¶23 in proposal B05-07.

rejected_barriers.quote: then he threw on a quantity of wood
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s (and Homer’s, 5.257) unexplained detail, whose purpose is disputed. Explaining it would add interpretation.

rejected_barriers.quote: a goatskin full of black wine
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: keep the Bear on his left
rejected_barriers.reason: The candidate’s reordering (Calypso’s instruction first) keeps Butler’s logic. The next sentence identifies the Bear as stars, and the reader worked it out.

rejected_barriers.quote: the Pleiads, on late-setting Bootes
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s star names. They need outside knowledge only.

rejected_barriers.quote: Men also call it the Wain
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s own gloss, capitalized by ruling (continuity §5, finding 21.2), and read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: alone never dips into the stream of Oceanus
rejected_barriers.reason: A name and a piece of cosmology that need outside knowledge only. The sense (it never sets) was read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: facing Orion
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s name for the constellation. The double reference is the poem’s.

rejected_barriers.quote: rising like a shield on the horizon
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s image, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: it made him very angry
rejected_barriers.reason: Poseidon’s grudge is set up in Book 1 and told in Book 9 (see the context note), so this is not a defect of Book 5.

rejected_barriers.quote: returning from the Ethiopians
rejected_barriers.reason: A name, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: fell on him
rejected_barriers.reason: A pronoun reference the reader resolved. Butler’s wording.

rejected_barriers.quote: How black Zeus is making heaven with his clouds
rejected_barriers.reason: Odysseus blames Zeus for Poseidon’s storm in Butler and in Homer. ‘heaven’ is kept under the heaven census (continuity §3).

rejected_barriers.quote: those Danaans who fell before Troy in the cause of the sons of Atreus
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s names for the Greeks, kept (glossary name lists). They need outside knowledge only.

rejected_barriers.quote: the Achaeans would have honored my name
rejected_barriers.reason: A name, kept.

rejected_barriers.quote: the raft reeled again
rejected_barriers.reason: A real but harmless dead sense: Butler’s ‘again’ means ‘back, in response to the blow’, and it is read as ‘a second time’. The action (the wave strikes, the raft lurches, he goes overboard) is understood in full. Every one-word repair either collides or adds interpretation: ‘reeled back’ would put a second ‘back’ beside the candidate’s ‘batting it back and forth’ in the same paragraph, one modern word for two Butler items (D26); ‘reeled under it’ reuses Butler’s ‘under water’; ‘violently’ interprets. No proposal is made.

rejected_barriers.quote: He let go the helm
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s own variation for the steering gear (‘rudder’ in ¶19–20, ‘helm’ here). ‘helm’ is current English and was read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: as autumn winds whirl thistledown round and round on a road
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s image, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: leave your raft to drive before the wind
rejected_barriers.reason: A nautical phrase, decoded correctly. Butler’s concrete detail.

rejected_barriers.quote: and then go away again
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s phrasing (Homer: ‘turn away’). The meaning was recovered.

rejected_barriers.quote: as long as her timbers hold together
rejected_barriers.reason: A pronoun reference the reader resolved. Butler’s wording.

rejected_barriers.quote: a heap of dry chaff
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: till you fall in with well-to-do people
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly as Poseidon’s sarcasm. Butler’s wording.

rejected_barriers.quote: he lashed his horses and drove to Aegae
rejected_barriers.reason: Poseidon’s chariot is the poem’s. This is not a wording problem.

rejected_barriers.quote: bound the paths of all the winds
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s image (‘bound the ways’), read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: a good stiff breeze from the North that should lay the waters
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly (‘calm and flatten’), and ‘lay’ in this sense is current, as in ‘lay the dust’. The puzzle of a strong wind calming the sea is Butler’s (Homer: she ‘broke the waves before him’, 5.385), not the edition’s.

rejected_barriers.quote: as children rejoice when their dear father, who has long borne a sore affliction sent him by some angry spirit, begins to get better
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly. The candidate has already recast the simile into order.

rejected_barriers.quote: where a ship might ride
rejected_barriers.reason: Nautical, decoded correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: some shelving beach
rejected_barriers.reason: Decoded correctly. Butler’s concrete detail.

rejected_barriers.quote: for Amphitrite breeds many such
rejected_barriers.reason: A name that needs outside knowledge only.

rejected_barriers.quote: tearing his hands as the suckers of an octopus are torn when someone plucks it from its bed, and the stones come up along with it
rejected_barriers.reason: RULING, made against Butler: no repair. The inversion belongs to Homer and Butler, not to the edition. In the Greek (5.432–435), pebbles cling to the octopus’s suckers as it is dragged from its lair, and in the application the skin of Odysseus’s hands stays on the rock. What is torn away and what keeps the fragments change sides between the two halves. Butler renders it faithfully (‘the suckers of a polypus are torn … and the stones come up along with it—even so did the rocks tear the skin from his strong hands’). The candidate changes only ‘polypus’ → ‘octopus’ (continuity ruling) and divides the sentence at ‘Even so’. The reader describes the inversion exactly and paraphrases correctly, so there is no comprehension failure to repair, and straightening the simile would rewrite the poem. The sentence-initial ‘Even so did…’ that follows the division is kept: the inversion marks it as the second half of the comparison, and the edition keeps the same construction sentence-initially at 9 ¶25 (‘Even so did we bore…’).

rejected_barriers.quote: even in spite of his own destiny
rejected_barriers.reason: Homer’s idea (‘ὑπὲρ μόρον’, 5.436), read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: a spit that would take the waves aslant
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s coastal geography, decoded correctly (‘a narrow point of land where waves hit at an angle’). A spit of land is a current term, the clause explains it, and ‘aslant’ is transparent.

rejected_barriers.quote: He felt that there was a current, so he prayed inwardly
rejected_barriers.reason: ¶33–34 show the river god himself. Outside knowledge only.

rejected_barriers.quote: Hear me, O King, whoever you may be
rejected_barriers.reason: ‘your stream’ resolves it. Butler’s wording.

rejected_barriers.quote: cling to the knees of your riverhood
rejected_barriers.reason: The prior screening ruling (2026-09-23; continuity §5, B05-P034) is upheld. The reader decoded ‘riverhood’ exactly, as a coined honorific like ‘your majesty’ applied to the river, which is Butler’s point (Homer: ‘I come to your stream and your knees’). No comprehension failure outweighs the ruling. The supplication custom is cultural, not a wording problem, and Book 6 shows it in action; a gloss would add interpretation.

rejected_barriers.quote: I declare myself your suppliant
rejected_barriers.reason: Decoded correctly. Book 6 shows the custom, and a gloss would add interpretation.

rejected_barriers.quote: he took off the scarf that Ino had given him
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler’s own variation for one object (‘veil’ in ¶25 and ¶27, ‘scarf’ here), and the reader identified it. Kept as Butler wrote it.

rejected_barriers.quote: threw it back into the salt stream of the river

summary: Book 5 can be understood as it stands. The blind reader’s paraphrase is correct in all 37 paragraphs, and 88 of the 97 barriers are pauses over names and myths that Books 1–4 set up, tensions that are Butler’s own (who raised which storm; Calypso’s ‘come inside’), or technical vocabulary that the reader decoded and that stays as Butler’s concrete detail. There are nine real failures, all at word level: one blocking false friend (the sea-crows that ‘do their business in the waters’, ¶5); two constructions that can reverse an argument or an action (‘not one … but has forgotten’, ¶1; ‘pressing me … about the dead body’, ¶22); four words whose dominant modern sense blanks the picture of the raft, the wreck and the closing simile (‘hurdles’, ‘sheets’, ‘yard’, ‘brand’); and two optional items (‘a sea’ for a wave, ‘stayed’ for stopped). Every repair keeps Butler’s objects, and his words where they are still current. The source-aware sweep found no failure the reader had not flagged. Rulings: the inversion in the octopus simile belongs to Homer and Butler and is not straightened; the 2026-09-23 rulings on ‘riverhood’, ‘thrice-plowed’ and ‘adze’ are upheld; ‘presently’, ‘mischief’, ‘near of kin’ and the sacrificial ‘victims’ are kept, consistent with the rest of the edition. Paragraph numbers are 0-based, as in the pairs files.
